items.title: CVE-2026-111497: Node2Shell / HTTP2Shell Vulnerability May Allow RCE
items.summary: IntroductionOn October 21, 2026, the Node.js project disclosed CVE-2026-111497, an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in Google’s Brotli decoder used by Node.js and other software. The vulnerability is also known as Node2Shell and more recently as HTTP2Shell. The CVE score, filed by Google as the numbering authority, is 9.2 (Critical) on CVSS 4.0. The flaw can be triggered when a vulnerable process decompresses attacker-controlled Brotli data. Successful exploitation may result in process crashes, disclosure of process memory, or remote code execution (RCE). Imperva reported demonstrating code execution in fresh containers running the official Node.js 24.22.0 Linux arm64 image, with multiple attempts required in its test environment. The vulnerable Brotli decoder may be present in a range of runtimes, libraries, and software packages, including Node.js, Bun, Python Brotli bindings, .NET, Envoy Proxy, Istio, Java brotli4j, libbrotli, curl/libcurl through Brotli dependencies, and Linux distribution packages. Applications may be exposed if they decompress attacker-controlled data using a vulnerable decoder. The vulnerability may be reachable through both inbound and outbound traffic paths. A malicious client could send a crafted request with Content-Encoding: br to a vulnerable server-side component that performs Brotli request decompression. Conversely, a malicious or compromised server could return a crafted Brotli-compressed response to a vulnerable client application that automatically decodes Brotli responses. ThreatLabz has observed reconnaissance and exploitation attempts targeting this vulnerability through Zscaler Deception, as detailed in the ThreatLabz Observations section below. RecommendationsZscaler recommends the following measures to address CVE-2026-111497 and monitor for potentially related activity:Patch vulnerable runtimes and libraries. Upgrade vulnerable runtimes, packages, and infrastructure components to the patched versions listed in the Vulnerable Versions table. Prioritize services that decompress untrusted Brotli data, including internet-facing applications that accept compressed request bodies and services that fetch content from external or user-controlled URLs. Validate each vulnerable component independently. Updating the system-wide libbrotli package may not remediate applications that statically bundle Brotli or ship their own decoder copy.Rebuild and redeploy containers. Use patched base images, runtimes, and libraries, and verify the versions in running workloads. Updating a host’s libraries does not update copies bundled within container images.Disable Brotli decoding where patching is delayed. If immediate patching is not possible, disable Brotli decompression on vulnerable paths where supported, following vendor guidance and testing for application compatibility.Monitor for exploitation and post-exploitation behavior. Investigate the following: Unexpected process crashes in Node.js, Bun, Python, .NET, Envoy Proxy, or service mesh workloads.Repeated malformed Brotli payloads.Requests containing Content-Encoding: br to endpoints that normally do not receive compressed request bodies.Abnormal memory access violations or segmentation faults.Web server or application worker crashes after compressed request handling.Unexpected child processes spawned by web application runtimes.Unexpected outbound connections following crashes or the processing of malformed compressed input. Vulnerable VersionsThe following table lists vulnerable versions and corresponding fixes for selected software that incorporates the Brotli decoder. ProductVulnerable VersionsPatched VersionsGoogle Brotli1.0.3 < 1.0.10 (semver)1.0.10Google Brotli1.1.0 < 1.1.1 (semver)1.1.1Google Brotli1.2.0 < 1.2.1 (semver)1.2.1Node.js22.0.0 - 22.23.322.23.4Node.js24.0.0 - 24.22.024.22.1Node.js26.0.0 - 26.12.026.12.1Bun< 1.4.41.4.4.NET8.0.0 - 8.0.328.0.33.NET9.0.0 - 9.0.219.0.22.NET10.0.0 - 10.0.1310.0.14.NET11.0.0-preview.1 - 11.0.0-rc.211.0.0-rc.3.26522.148Python Brotli (PyPI)1.2.01.2.1Python brotlicffi (PyPI)1.2.0.0 - 1.2.0.21.2.1.0Envoy Proxy1.39.2, 1.38.5, 1.37.7, 1.36.111.40.0, 1.39.3, 1.38.6, 1.37.8, 1.36.12Java brotli4j< 1.24.01.24.0libbrotli (Debian)1.1.0-21.1.0-2+deb13u1libbrotliVaries by distributionApply vendor security updatesTable 1: Software versions vulnerable to CVE-2026-111497 and the corresponding patched versions.  ThreatLabz ObservationsThreatLabz observed reconnaissance and exploitation attempts involving CVE-2026-111497 through Zscaler Deception. Within the first 24 hours following public disclosure, Zscaler Deception’s global decoy mesh observed activity from 20 source IP addresses targeting 12 customers across 402 events. Of these events, 40% involved reconnaissance and 60% involved exploitation attempts. The table below summarizes the unique payloads associated with reconnaissance and exploitation attempts targeting CVE-2026-111497 observed through Zscaler Deception.Payload DescriptionJA4 FingerprintMalformed Brotli stream headers + valid Brotli differential check + Node.js path recont13d4312h1_c7886603b240_b26ce05bbdd6Truncated JSON Brotli + 8-byte invalid Brotli padding stream + uncompressed controlsNone22-byte & 23-byte invalid block-switch OOB-write seeds (CVE-2026-111497)t13d251100_b78ed14e2fd0_ab7e3b40a677Brotli decompression bomb / Celery stream probe + 1B controlsNoneAssetnote 1-byte malformed/valid Brotli differential checkMultiple observed3-stage Node2Shell capability, Strapi & CVE-2026-111497 JSON parser probet13d521100_b262b3658495_8e6e362c5eac14-byte Brotli {"ping":1} differential sweept13d1714h1_ab0a1bf427ad_5e078a691127Table 2: Unique payloads observed during reconnaissance and exploitation attempts targeting CVE-2026-111497. How It WorksBrotli is a lossless compression algorithm and data format developed by Google. It is used for HTTP compression to reduce the size of web content such as HTML, CSS, JavaScript, JSON, and API responses. Brotli-encoded HTTP content is identified by the Content-Encoding: br header.Applications may use Brotli directly or through dependencies such as runtimes, frameworks, HTTP clients, and middleware. In some configurations, these components automatically decompress Brotli-encoded content without application code explicitly calling Brotli APIs.Vulnerability detailsThe flaw occurs in Brotli’s block-decoding logic. When a stream changes block type, the decoder determines the next block type and length. In vulnerable versions, there is a macro (in the fast-path logic) that does not properly check the return value of the DecodeBlockTypeAndLength function, which can cause the decoder to continue processing an invalid state (e.g., when provided a maliciously crafted Brotli stream). This can lead to an out-of-bounds write and be used as a primitive for RCE. The upstream fix modifies the decoder so malformed block-switch conditions return a distinct error that is propagated to the caller, stopping further decoding of the malicious Brotli stream.Attack chainExploitation of CVE-2026-111497 may follow either an inbound or outbound path, depending on where Brotli decompression occurs, as shown in the figure below. Inbound attempts use crafted Brotli-compressed HTTP request bodies while outbound attempts use crafted responses returned by an attacker-controlled or compromised server. These responses may be consumed through fetch(), webhook delivery, URL previews, crawlers or scrapers, and API integrations. In either path, exploitation requires attacker-controlled Brotli data to reach a vulnerable decoder, with compressed HTTP content marked by Content-Encoding: br. Figure 1: Potential inbound and outbound exploitation paths for CVE-2026-111497. ConclusionCVE-2026-111497 affects the Brotli decoder used by Node.js and other software. Exposure depends on whether an application passes attacker-controlled Brotli data to a vulnerable decoder. Organizations should identify vulnerable components and apply corresponding vendor updates, including updates for applications that bundle their own copy of Brotli.Zscaler Deception has observed active reconnaissance and exploitation attempts involving this vulnerability. ThreatLabz will continue monitoring for related activity and provide updates as additional findings become available. Zscaler CoverageThe Zscaler ThreatLabz team has deployed protections for CVE-2026-111497 with the following signatures:Zscaler Private Access (ZPA) App ProtectionThe following ZPA App Protection signature detects attempts to exploit CVE-2026-111497 in internal applications accessed through ZPA, including activity originating from compromised endpoints or insiders:6000572: Node2Shell - Brotli Decoder Buffer Overflow (CVE-2026-111497)Zscaler Advanced Threat ProtectionApp.Exploit.CVE-2026-111497Zscaler Deception Organizations should deploy the following Zscaler Deception decoys to help detect reconnaissance and exploitation attempts:MLflowMetaflowBento FrontendRay ServeGitLab How Zscaler Can HelpThe following table shows the typical attack stages and the mitigations recommended by Zscaler.Attack StageRecommended MitigationMinimize the external attack surfaceIdentify internet-facing applications containing vulnerable versions using Zscaler Exposure Management.Find services running vulnerable runtimes or libraries.Reduce direct exposure by placing applications behind a Zero Trust architecture.Prevent compromiseEnable SSL/TLS inspection where appropriate. Use Advanced Threat Protection to detect exploit attempts and suspicious payload delivery. Use ZPA App Protection to inspect and block suspicious requests targeting private applications. Reduce outbound exploitation riskRoute server egress through Zscaler Internet Access (ZIA) to inspect outbound traffic.Restrict application egress to approved destinations. Pay special attention to webhook, crawler, URL preview, and third-party integration services that fetch content from external or user-controlled URLs.Prevent lateral threat movementUse ZPA to enforce least-privilege user-to-application segmentation.Use Zscaler Deception to detect attacker movement after initial compromise. Monitor for suspicious access to internal applications following web application crashes or abnormal behavior.Detect post-exploitation activityUse Zscaler Managed Detection & Response (MDR) and Threat Hunting to investigate suspicious process behavior, command execution, unusual outbound connections, container runtime anomalies, and web application worker crashes.Prevent data lossInspect outbound traffic across channels with Zscaler Data Loss Prevention (DLP).Monitor for unusual uploads, archive transfers, credential exposure, or data movement following suspected exploitation. CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619: PHP Vulnerable to Unauthenticated RCE Attacks
items.summary:
*October 26, 2026: This advisory has been updated to clarify language describing exploitability and potential impact.*October 23, 2026: This advisory has been updated with new ThreatLabz analysis and Zscaler Deception telemetry on exploitation activity observed during the first 48 hours following disclosure.IntroductionOn October 21, 2026, two critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, collectively referred to as “PHP2Shell,” were publicly disclosed. Both vulnerabilities carry a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2 out of 10. The PHP security team has released emergency patches and strongly encouraged all PHP users to update immediately. These flaws reside in the PHP core language runtime and successful exploitation could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to achieve remote code execution on any server running a vulnerable version, potentially enabling unauthorized access, data theft, or further system compromise. Given PHP's pervasive deployment across web infrastructure globally - including applications like WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, and Magento, as well as embedded devices and similarly overlooked public-facing platforms - the potential attack surface is significant. The vulnerabilities could enable automated exploitation of exposed, vulnerable PHP deployments without authentication or user interaction. The vulnerabilities therefore may be attractive targets for exploitation.ThreatLabz analysis indicates that attackers began rapidly targeting these vulnerabilities following public disclosure, highlighting the need for organizations to patch vulnerable PHP deployments immediately.Zscaler’s security team has analyzed this issue across both production and corporate environments and has ruled out any impact to Zscaler Cloud Platforms, products, distributed components, services, or our enterprise environment, as detailed in the Trust post.For more on PHP2Shell and its implications for enterprise security, watch our webinar with EVP, Cybersecurity Deepen Desai and Director of Threat Research Jithin Nair. RecommendationsOrganizations running PHP should take the following actions:Patch immediately: Upgrade PHP to one of the fixed versions: 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35. Linux package maintainers received patches in advance and may already have updated packages available. PHP packages for most Linux distributions may also include the patches backported to previous versions of the software, so consult the release notes for your specific installation to ensure your systems are covered.Deactivate unpatched instances: Consider fully disabling services for any PHP instance that cannot be immediately patched. While this may seem overly cautious, any unpatched instance could be targeted by opportunistic adversaries and result in shell-level access to the vulnerable host. Inventory PHP deployments: Conduct an immediate inventory of all PHP installations across your environment, including standalone servers, vendor appliances, bundled software (WordPress, Magento, WooCommerce, Shopware), and hosting panels (cPanel, Plesk, etc).Migrate off EOL branches: Organizations running PHP 5.4+, 7.x, 8.0, or 8.1 must migrate to a supported branch immediately. No official binary patches will be released for these versions.Isolate EOL instances that cannot be immediately migrated: Migrating EOL instances is strongly recommended. If this is not possible, isolating unpatchable applications from the internet and other untrusted networks may provide some level of protection. This should be considered a high-risk mitigation and reserved only for business and mission-critical applications while implementing aggressive monitoring of these instances.Monitor for exploitation: Audit web server logs (including but not limited to Apache, Nginx, etc.) for unusual segmentation faults, crash dumps, or abnormal memory usage patterns that may indicate active exploitation attempts.Mitigate risk through PHP settings: While not a definitive fix, mission critical applications that cannot be disabled or immediately patched may benefit from reviewing and tightening memory_limit and max_execution_time settings in php.ini to avoid triggering OOM conditions. Consult additional guidance regarding mitigations through setting session.upload_progress.enabled = Off and disabling multipart uploads at the service edge. ThreatLabz Observes Exploitation Attempts Within 48 HoursThreatLabz observed scanning activity and possible exploitation attempts targeting the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities using multiple attack tools and exploitation methods, including RCE payloads, PHP object injection, and named exploitation frameworks, indicating rapid, in-the-wild exploitation attempts.In the first 48 hours after the PHP2Shell disclosure, Zscaler’s global decoy mesh observed 1,156 exploitation attempts from 156 unique attacker IPs targeting 70 organizations. As a rapid response measure, a new detection rule for PHP2Shell exploitation has been pushed to all Zscaler Deception customers.Attack chainAutomated scanning activity observed by Zscaler suggests attackers may be attempting to use a two-stage PHP2Shell exploitation chain, as shown in the figure below.Figure 1: Notional exploit chain consistent with scanning and exploit attempts observed by ThreatLabz.Stage 1: State setup and fatal triggerThe attacker sends a crafted multipart/form-data POST request containing:A PHPSESSID field to associate the request with a known session, making the session filename (sess_[PHPSESSID]) predictable.The PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS field to force PHP to begin session bookkeeping during multipart parsing, populating vulnerable global state pointers and writing attacker-controlled data into the session file.A file attachment whose filename= parameter contains either PHP code or a serialized object string.A body sized or structured to exhaust memory (CVE-2026-109618) or trigger a fatal error (CVE-2026-109619).When the fatal condition is triggered, longjmp() aborts the request, freeing per-request memory but leaving stale global pointers.Stage 2: Heap reclaim and code executionThe attacker immediately sends a second request to the same worker process. This second request contains the attacker's payload, sized and aligned to reclaim the freed memory slots. When PHP processes the new request and references the stale global state before re-initialization occurs, it reads and executes the attacker-controlled data, achieving arbitrary code execution with the privileges of the PHP worker process.Zscaler Deception telemetry findingsThreatLabz observed malicious POST requests targeting the PHP2Shell exploitation path across multiple tools and stages of the attack chain. Every observed request is a multipart/form-data POST targeting PHP endpoints, specifically /, /index.php, /api/endpoint.php, and /app/upload.php.Exploitation payloads observed1. ShellFlow PHP2Shell named exploit toolThe most forensically significant artifact is the presence of a multipart boundary string that explicitly names the exploitation tool. This indicator should not be considered durable, as an adversary can trivially replace the known strings with something less obvious. At this time, the ShellFlow tool uses a known boundary value, so it is a useful indicator for detecting the unmodified tool. The exploit tool request is shown below. POST / HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=----shellflow-php2shell

------shellflow-php2shell
Content-Disposition: form-data; name="PHPSESSID"

sf618_ec172709c8b74601
------shellflow-php2shell
Content-Disposition: form-data; name="PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS"
shellflow_poc

------shellflow-php2shell
Content-Disposition: form-data; name="f"; filename="poc.bin"
Content-Type: application/octet-stream

AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA[...15485 bytes total...]The multipart boundary shellflow-php2shell identifies the attacking tool by name. The poc.bin file body contains more than 15k bytes of data along with a repeated AAAA... characters, a characteristic heap spray pattern used for memory layout control in the CVE-2026-109618 OOM corruption path.Notable characteristics:The boundary string shellflow-php2shell directly identifies the ShellFlow PHP2Shell attacking tool, which is publicly linked to CVE-2026-109618 scanning activity.The session ID sf618_ec172709c8b74601 contains sf618, possibly reflecting a developer’s shorthand reference to ShellFlow + CVE-2026-109618.The application/octet-stream upload with a repeating AAAAA... buffer is consistent with a heap spray technique used to influence the memory layout when the OOM condition is triggered.2. Active system() command execution payloadThese requests represent the strongest indication of automated exploitation attempts. The filename= field contains a fully formed PHP webshell instruction designed to be written into the PHP session file through the session.upload_progress handler and later executed, as shown in the example below.The filename= value [?php system('echo 'exploited digga' > pwned.txt');echo 'RCE';?] instructs the PHP runtime to:Execute the OS command echo 'exploited digga' > pwned.txt, writing a proof-of-compromise marker to disk.Echo the string RCE in the HTTP response body, providing an indication of successful code execution to the attacker. The RCE string may still be returned even if the preceding echo redirection fails.This payload pattern was observed in two separate requests with identical content, consistent with automated retry behavior commonly seen in exploit frameworks.3. PHP object injection via pipe delimiterThreatLabz also observed a PHP object injection request that abuses the session pipe delimiter, as shown in the example. The filename x|O:8:"stdClass":0:{} uses the PHP default session serialization format, where the | character separates a variable name from its serialized value.POST /app/upload.php HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=--NeoMM2026
--NeoMM2026
Content-Disposition: form-data; name="PHPSESSID"

--NeoMM2026
Content-Disposition: form-data; name="PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS"

--NeoMM2026
Content-Disposition: form-data; name="f"; filename="x|O:8:\"stdClass\":0:{}"
Content-Type: text/plain

--NeoMM2026--Overall attack tool fingerprinting summaryThreatLabz identified multiple distinct attacker toolsets through analysis of numerous requests in our telemetry, as summarized in the table below:Tool / FrameworkIdentifying MarkersShellFlow PHP2ShellBoundary shellflow-php2shell; session ID prefix sf618; poc.bin heap sprayActive RCE OperatorBoundary --VERIFY; system() payload in filename=; pwned.txt writeNuclei CVE TemplatesBoundary prefix ------Nuclei; echo-test random token in filenameNeo ScannerBoundary --NeoMM2026b / --NeoMM2026; targets /api/endpoint.php, /app/upload.phpTable 1: Attacker tools and identifying markers observed in PHP2Shell exploitation activity. Affected VersionsAll PHP versions from 5.4 onward are vulnerable. Only currently supported branches received patches, but package maintainers may also backport the security patches to previous versions. Carefully review the instructions and release notes from the maintainers of your PHP installations to determine what version and release includes the necessary patch.PHP BranchVulnerable VersionsPatch AvailablePHP 8.58.5.0 – 8.5.11Yes (8.5.12)PHP 8.48.4.0 – 8.4.26Yes (8.4.27)PHP 8.38.3.0 – 8.3.35Yes (8.3.36)PHP 8.28.2.0 – 8.2.34Yes (8.2.35)PHP 8.1All versions (EOL)No (EOL — upgrade required)PHP 8.0All versions (EOL)No (EOL — upgrade required)PHP 7.xAll versions (EOL)No (EOL — upgrade required)PHP 5.4+All versions (EOL)No (EOL — upgrade required)Table 2: CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 Affected PHP Versions and Patch Availability How It WorksBoth vulnerabilities are use-after-free memory safety flaws in PHP's core request-handling engine. All PHP installations serving web requests may be affected regardless of security controls. The vulnerabilities can allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code on affected servers or read sensitive process memory; that memory may contain passwords, authentication tokens, API keys and certificates belonging to other requests or the server itself.CVE-2026-109618: OOM Corruption / Uninitialized Memory UseCVSS v4.0: 9.2 - CriticalRoot Cause: PHP uses longjmp() to abort a request when it hits its configured memory limit. When a web application receives form input, PHP records new entries in its internal POST data structure before finishing their initialization. If an out-of-memory (OOM) error fires while internal request data is only partially initialized, longjmp() bypasses normal control flow, leaving memory in an inconsistent/uninitialized state. During request cleanup, PHP misinterprets this invalid data as valid and follows an attacker-controlled code pointer, yielding control of execution.Exploit Vector: An attacker can intentionally trigger specific OOM conditions (e.g., via large memory allocations, deeply recursive calls, or maliciously crafted request payloads) to corrupt state and achieve unauthenticated RCE.Impact: Unauthenticated Remote Code ExecutionCVE-2026-109619: Use-After-Free / Stale Memory AccessCVSS v4.0: 9.2 - CriticalRoot Cause: When PHP encounters a fatal error and calls zend_bailout() (via longjmp()), request-owned internal state can survive in global memory after its backing allocation has been freed. PHP workers process multiple requests in sequence, and certain internal pointers persist between requests. If a request crashes or exhausts memory at the right moment, those pointers are left pointing to already-recycled memory. A subsequent request processed by the same worker may access this stale memory before re-initialization occurs.Exploit Vector: This vulnerability is chainable with CVE-2026-109618. The partial initialization in CVE-2026-109618 allows an attacker to shape the freed memory contents and gain control of the instruction pointer, potentially enabling RCE. Chaining these two CVEs requires no authentication and no user interaction.Impact: Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution and memory/credential disclosure ConclusionPHP2Shell represents a significant security issue because of the severity of the vulnerabilities and PHP’s broad deployment. The combination of CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 could provide an unauthenticated path to RCE and potentially broader server compromise without user interaction.Organizations are strongly urged to treat this as an emergency patching event. Systems running EOL PHP branches must be migrated without delay. Where patching cannot be completed immediately, network-layer controls should be applied as an interim measure.ThreatLabz will continue to monitor active exploitation campaigns and update Zscaler platform protections as new indicators emerge. How Zscaler Can HelpThe following table shows the typical attack stages and the mitigations recommended by Zscaler.Attack StageRecommended MitigationMinimize the external attack surfaceIdentify and fix any vulnerable PHP applications with Zscaler Exposure ManagementEliminate externally exposed PHP assets by leveraging a Zero Trust architecture.Prevent compromiseDetonate unknown second-stage payloads with Advanced Cloud Sandbox.Route server egress through ZIA to detect/block post-compromise activity.Enable SSL/TLS inspection for all traffic, including trusted sources.Enable Advanced Threat Protection to block known C2 domains.Use Advanced Cloud Firewall, to extend C2 controls across all ports/protocols, including emerging C2.Prevent lateral threat movementUse ZPA to enforce least-privilege user-to-app segmentation for crown-jewel apps (employees and third parties).Use ZPA inline inspection to block exploitation attempts against private apps from compromised users.Use Zscaler Deception to detect and contain lateral movement or privilege escalation with decoy assets and accounts.Use Zscaler MDR and Threat Hunting to detect and respond to early stage threat activity.Prevent data lossInspect outbound traffic across channels with Zscaler DLP. Zscaler CoverageThe Zscaler ThreatLabz team has deployed protections for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 with the following signatures:Zscaler Advanced Threat ProtectionThe Zscaler Advanced Threat Protection signatures detect exploitation attempts from ZIA traffic targeting internet-exposed servers:PHP.Exploit.CVE-2026-109618_19Zscaler Private Access AppProtectionThe ZPA App Protection signatures detect exploitation attempts against internal applications through ZPA, including activity originating from compromised endpoints or insiders:6000568: PHP Remote Code Execution (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619)6000569: PHP2Shell Excessive Multipart Parts (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619)Zscaler Deception Zscaler Deception customers can deploy Private Threat Intelligence decoys for the following applications to detect PHP2Shell exploitation attempts and generate high-fidelity alerts:WordPress LoginDrupal Admin PanelJoomla Admin PanelphpMyAdminNextcloudCustomers can configure an orchestration rule to add any IP addresses interacting with these decoys to a firewall block list.Zscaler MDRZscaler MDR's behavioral detection analytics also provide generic coverage for this class of web application RCE. The following active detection analytics are candidates for identifying post-exploitation activity that may result from these vulnerabilities:NIX-WEBSERVER-SPAWN-SUSPICIOUS-COMMAND — Linux web servers spawning suspicious commands including reconnaissance utilities and downloadersNIX-WEBSERVER-SPAWN-RECON — Web servers spawning reconnaissance commandsPSX-WEBSERVER-CREATE-PHP-SCRIPT — Web servers creating inline PHP scripts in web directories Indicators Of Compromise (IOCs)Zscaler Deception observed IP addresses delivering PHP2Shell-related payloads. Selected source IP addresses and their associated activity are listed below.IP AddressObserved activity169[.]58[.]138[.]154Nuclei code-injection + deserialization check23[.]226[.]136[.]36OOM / memory-exhaustion trigger (CVE-2026-109618)78[.]17[.]70[.]38 OS command exec + file write135[.]136[.]21[.]120 Persistent webshell81[.]17[.]100[.]107Real deserialization RCE gadget chains (phpggc)The full list of source IP addresses and JA4 fingerprints observed in this activity are available in the ThreatLabz GitHub repository.Contributors: Abhishek Parikh, Deepak Keshav, Prajjwal Singh, Sayan Mitra, Nataraja Gundale, Rishabh Nihalani, Sai Nikhil Perla, Rubin Azad

items.title: Inside a Global AI-Assisted Hacking Campaign
items.summary:
IntroductionIn October 2026, Zscaler ThreatLabz investigated AI-assisted cyberattacks that combined the ARTEX penetration testing framework with AI coding assistants and custom automation scripts. Initial reporting of the incident identified the targeting of South Korean financial institutions. However, ThreatLabz discovered additional information about the attack, which went far beyond South Korea. The AI-assisted attacks were widespread and targeted organizations around the globe and in multiple industry sectors.In this blog post, ThreatLabz examines the operator’s working environment, explains the roles assigned to AI models and tools, and analyzes the targeting and objectives reflected in the operator’s prompts. Key TakeawaysIn October 2026, ThreatLabz discovered information about an AI-assisted attack combining a customized ARTEX deployment with Claude Code, Codex, and Grok workspaces. Custom scripts shared instructions and supported handoffs between AI sessions.ARTEX was configured to use a DeepSeek model through an OpenAI-compatible gateway, but other configurations also specified DeepSeek, GLM, and Grok.Prompts directed AI models to divide investigation tasks and review one another’s findings, including instructions for GLM to review work performed by DeepSeek and its subagents.Saved project records and synchronization scripts were designed to preserve investigation context and progress across accounts, servers, and AI sessions. Prompt histories revealed targeting across multiple industries and geographic regions. Requests for bulk personal and transaction data, alongside questions about selling stolen data, suggest the attacks were financially motivated. BackgroundThreatLabz identified an ARTEX deployment that included AI assistant configurations, synchronization scripts, network routing tools, and a Claude Code prompt history. The recorded prompts spanned August 4 through October 4, 2026 (UTC). CrowdStrike separately reported on related ARTEX infrastructure and the targeting of South Korean financial organizations on October 7, 2026. This blog examines the broader working environment of the attacks and targets. Operator InfrastructureThe figure below illustrates the threat actor’s environment based on saved configurations and instructions.Figure 1: Architectural diagram of AI-assisted attack environment using ARTEX. Technical AnalysisThe following sections examine the operator’s infrastructure, customized tooling, AI environment configuration, and targeting objectives, offering a closer look at the workflow behind the campaign.Work server and jump serverAs Recorded Future detailed in their recent blog post, the operator's work server stored project files, scripts, AI settings, and a local ARTEX deployment. The jump server, 38.244.50.120, served as the default route for connections to targets.The jump server also ran additional AI sessions. The operator delegated research tasks to Grok on that server and instructed a separate AI session to review Grok’s findings. This setup divided work between the two servers, with the operator providing oversight and direction. Three custom scripts synchronized shared AI instructions and supporting files across accounts, which are described in the table below.Script namePurposetools/sync-all.shUses SSH and rsync to copy AI instructions, reusable task guides, saved notes, and tools to the jump server's root, claude, grok, and gemini accounts.sync-memory.shCopies saved AI notes, known as memory files, to locations on the jump server.tools/sync-cc-users.shCopies shared Claude Code instructions and supporting files to the gemini and glm accounts on the work server.Table 1: Custom synchronization scripts and their purposes for AI-assisted attacks.Each account maintained its own AI service settings. The synchronization scripts were designed to update model references within specialist agent instructions to match the destination account, allowing the workspaces to use shared instructions with different model configurations.The scripts also incorporated backups and validation checks designed to avoid overwriting modified destination files. These mechanisms indicate that the operator intended to keep configurations consistent across environments.Customized ARTEX deploymentARTEX is an AI-assisted penetration-testing framework. Its planner-and-worker architecture lets an operator define a goal, which AI agents break down into tasks, execute using tools, and document by retaining assets and findings for review. The recovered deployment extends the framework with additional tools for web, network, and Android analysis.The saved Docker Compose file defines an ARTEX container and a PostgreSQL 16 database. It configured the ARTEX interface to use host port 8890 and mapped PostgreSQL to 127.0.0.1:5435. The ARTEX container uses a custom image tagged artex-local:perf2-20261003. The corresponding Dockerfile adds tools including nmap, sqlmap, nuclei, httpx, jadx, apktool, and frida-tools. It also adds Python libraries for web processing and spreadsheet output and replaces the original ARTEX program with the operator’s local version.AI model setupThe operator changed model routing over time and used account names that did not always match the configured model. To understand this setup, it is important to distinguish the client application, such as Claude Code, from the model service receiving its requests.For example, the saved ARTEX environment configuration specifies:ARTEX_LLM_PROVIDER=openai
ARTEX_LLM_MODEL=deepseek-v4.1-flash
ARTEX_LLM_BASE_URL=https://xcai.pro/v1Here, openai specifies an OpenAI-compatible API format. The model field requests deepseek-v4.1-flash, while the base URL routes requests to xcai.pro. These settings identify the requested model and gateway endpoint, but do not confirm which underlying model the gateway actually served.The table below summarizes the model assignments recorded in the collected configurations. Model names are reproduced as requested IDs and were not independently verified.Workspace or componentRequested model IDsRoleARTEX local deploymentdeepseek-v4.1-flashModel backend for ARTEX's task workflow, configured through https://xcai.pro/v1.Codex (.codex/config.toml)deepseek-v4-proAlternative coding-agent interface configured to send requests to https://api.deepseek.com/v1.Local account named gemini, running Claude Codedeepseek-v4.1-flashWorkspace using shared instructions and specialist agents.Local account named glm, running Claude Codeglm-5.3Workspace configured to request GLM and use the shared workflow.Jump-host accounts named root and claudeglm-5.3, glm-5.3-flashAssigned analyzer and collector roles in the jump-host synchronization script.Jump-host account named grokgrok-4.7-xhigh, grok-4.7-build-fastAssigned analyzer and collector roles; operator also requested remote research and continued auditing.Jump-host account named gemini xcai/deepseek-v4.1-flashWorkspace the operator explicitly requested to reconfigure to use DeepSeek.Table 2: AI model configuration and assigned roles used in the AI-assisted attacks.In some instances, the threat actor assigned distinct roles to individual AI models. The prompt history includes instructions for DeepSeek to conduct the initial investigation, followed by GLM reviewing the findings for potential gaps. One translated prompt states: "When DeepSeek says it has exhausted all attack surfaces and I say to start a GLM review, GLM should review DeepSeek's previous work and its subagents' work."Later prompts assigned GLM additional investigation tasks, extending its intended role beyond reviewing DeepSeek’s findings.The operator requested both Grok’s native terminal application and a Claude Code setup configured to use Grok as its underlying AI model. For the Claude Code integration, the operator installed a bridge service called grok2api on the jump server. Prompts assigned extensive research tasks to Grok on that server and other AI sessions to review its output. The prompt history shows repeated requests to modify this configuration, but the specific setup used for each task could not be confirmed.The records establish the use of the Claude Code application, with configurations specifying DeepSeek, GLM, and Grok. However, since the underlying model responding to each session could not be independently verified, it's possible that some sessions used Anthropic’s Claude models.Persistent project stateThe operator organized each investigation into a separate folder. A script created files to record targets, testing progress, notes, vulnerability reports, and supporting evidence. These records provided context that an AI assistant could read to resume an investigation in a later session.File or folderWhat it recordsscope.mdWebsites, servers, or applications selected for investigation.surface.mdDiscovered pages, APIs, and other entry points, including their testing status.notes.mdCompleted work, decisions, and next steps.findings/Reports on potential or confirmed vulnerabilities.evidence/Supporting files, such as captured responses and tool output.Table 3: AI-assisted attack investigation files and folders and their purposes.The operator also configured a mechanism to help AI sessions retain context, track progress, divide tasks, and resume work started in other sessions:Provide project context with each prompt: An automated hook script (tools/project_context_hook.py) was configured to execute when a new prompt was received, read the current project files, and attach a brief summary of testing status, recent notes, and paths to relevant memory files. This provided context to help the AI continue previous work.Distribute tasks among specialized AI agents: The operator created tailored instructions for agents assigned to discover APIs, review source code, or analyze Android applications. The primary AI session was directed to validate their outputs before recording them as confirmed findings.Reduce operator approval requirements: The instructions directed the AI to assume that all supplied targets were preauthorized. Some application settings also permitted autonomous actions without requiring explicit operator approval for each step.Facilitate cross-session handoffs: The operator configured Codex to ingest saved instructions and notes, allowing other accounts to access prior conversation histories. A task guide also instructed the AI running under the jump server's gemini account on how to take over an ARTEX task and review its results.Proxy exits, tunnels, and cloud backupThe operator instructed the AI tools to connect to targets through the jump server. Additional proxy configurations provided separate outbound IP addresses for individual projects, helping limit direct connections between the primary work server and target environments.SSH tunnels were configured to support bidirectional communication between the two servers for AI and file services. Background monitoring tasks were configured to restart supporting services and tunnels if they were interrupted.Investigation assets were archived to Backblaze B2, with reports, supporting evidence, source code, data exports, and backups organized into separate directories. This structure followed the operator's directive to separate each target's operational data from its final analysis report for easier retrieval.Target profile and objectivesThe prompt history showed targeting beyond South Korean financial institutions, including dating applications, SMS providers, cryptocurrency and payment platforms, gift-card portals, gambling sites, retail platforms, educational services, logistics companies, and legal settlement systems. The targets also spanned multiple geographic regions, suggesting an opportunistic approach. The recorded prompts included requests to scan or investigate organizations in Canada, China, Cuba, Hong Kong, India, Indonesia, Japan, Kazakhstan, Kenya, Malaysia, Nigeria, South Africa, South Korea, Taiwan, Thailand, the United Arab Emirates (UAE), the United Kingdom, the United States, and Vietnam. The figure below shows the geographic distribution of targets referenced in the operator’s prompt history.Figure 2: Geographic distribution of targets referenced in the AI-assisted attacks prompt history.The table below summarizes representative target categories and the desired outcomes requested in the threat actor's prompts:Target or sectorRequested outcome in the prompt historySocial and dating servicesCollect frontend files and subdomains; gain access to user records.SMS providersGain administrative access, obtain SMS-channel credentials, or identify ways to send unlimited messages at no cost.RetailObtain customer order data.EducationObtain course-purchase records or user data.Investment servicesReview prior investigation records and obtain current data.Cryptocurrency and digital assetsFind a vulnerability that would allow NFT gifts to be obtained for free.Legal claims administrationReview investigation records, analyze claim workflows, and assess opportunities for additional access.Table 4: Representative target sector categories and requested outcomes in AI-assisted attacks prompt history.Prompt histories indicate an explicit focus on obtaining structured personally identifiable information (PII) and mobile phone numbers. In one instance, the operator stated that database dumps lacking phone number fields were of no value and requested alternative injection methods. In another prompt, the operator questioned why a specific SQL query targeting demographic data for female users over 30 returned only approximately 300 records.The threat actor instructed AI models to decrypt encrypted fields, parse transaction histories, translate database schemas into Chinese, and remove irrelevant metadata. These requests suggest an intent to prepare datasets for monetization.Prompts about underground data marketplaces further support this assessment. In one example, the operator asked: "If hackers compromise Korean data, where do they usually sell it?"Additional prompts focused on extracting payment gateway API keys, exploiting NFT minting workflows, and gaining unauthorized administrative privileges.To reduce the risk of detection, the threat actor explicitly warned AI models not to initiate direct account withdrawals, noting that unauthorized financial transactions could trigger security alerts or create traceable records. Threat AttributionThe recovered records point to a Chinese-speaking operator. The operator wrote predominantly in Chinese, requested Chinese as the default response language, specified China Standard Time, and instructed the AI to translate exported data fields into Chinese. In discussions about SMS services and app downloads, the operator referred to Chinese services and applications as “domestic.” The operator also supplied the same mobile number in mainland China format for accounts with a Chinese proxy provider and a cloud-phone service.  ConclusionThis investigation shows how a threat actor combined open source security tools, AI assistants, and custom automation scripts to launch attacks globally. Shared project records, specialized agents, and instructions for reviewing other models’ findings created a workflow designed to continue investigations across AI sessions under the operator’s direction. The prompt history also revealed broad targeting and an emphasis on obtaining personal and financial data, indicating the attacks were likely financially motivated.To defend against AI-assisted attacks, organizations should adopt a Zero Trust architecture that minimizes internet exposure and enforces least-privilege access. The Zscaler Zero Trust Exchange supports these principles by making applications invisible to the public internet and restricting access to authorized users. Zscaler Exposure Management, part items.title: CVE-2026-88771: Inside the Exploitation of a Critical NetScaler RCE Vulnerability
Threat Actor Abuses Agentic AI Pentesting Framework to Target South Korean Financial Institutions
items.summary: IntroductionZscaler ThreatLabz analyzed a recently active exploitation campaign in which a threat actor abused ARTEX to target South Korean financial institutions. ARTEX is an open source agentic penetration testing framework developed in China that uses large language models (LLMs) to automate reconnaissance and exploitation tasks. First observed in late September 2026, the campaign affected multiple South Korean financial firms and resulted in the exfiltration of personally identifiable information (PII) belonging to approximately 67,000 individuals.ThreatLabz assesses with moderate confidence that the campaign is the work of a financially motivated, Chinese-speaking threat actor. The threat actor exploited peripheral internet-facing web applications, including customer-facing inquiry portals and employee-facing mobile application backends. RecommendationsThe threat actor used AI to support reconnaissance and exploitation in this campaign. ThreatLabz recommends the following practices to strengthen defenses against AI-assisted attacks. For additional context on AI-driven security testing, see our blog: When the Scanner Starts Thinking: Learnings from Mythos & GPT 5.5 Cyber in Security Testing.Reduce application exposure: Reduce your external exposure by moving your applications behind a Zero Trust access solution, like Zscaler Private Access (ZPA). Understand your assets and associated risks: Establish complete visibility into internet-facing and internal assets, including AI assets, and assess their exposure and vulnerabilities to prioritize remediation. Zscaler’s AI Asset Management, Asset Exposure Management, External Attack Surface Management, and Unified Vulnerability can support these efforts.Deploy deception controls: Use Zscaler Deception to detect suspicious reconnaissance and access attempts through decoy assets and accounts. Configure automatic containment to restrict the associated asset or identity’s access to production applications while capturing activity in the decoy environment.Prioritize Zero Trust everywhere architecture: Apply Zero Trust consistently across remote and on-premises environments. Enforce least-privilege user-to-application access to limit lateral propagation and reduce the blast radius from AI-driven attacks.Use AI red teaming and guardrails for your production models: Use AI red teaming and guardrails to assess susceptibility to prompt injection and unsafe outputs. Monitor for hallucinations and model drift over time.Use AI-powered exposure management: Use the Zscaler Exposure Management remediation agent to prioritize remediation and patching for high-risk exposures across external and internal assets.Alert on enumeration: On partner and employee portals, alert on sequential lookups and unusually high numbers of records accessed per session. Apply rate limits to affected endpoints. Enforce server-side authorization for access to customer records and limit responses to the fields required for the operation.Treat open source pentesting harnesses as hostile code: If your organization uses an open source pentesting harness, isolate it from production, avoid storing production credentials in it, and enforce testing scope through configuration and code rather than prompts alone. Review forks before execution. Use Zscaler’s open source Agentic Radar to map agent workflows from source code.Test authorization regularly: Repeat security testing as applications change, and verify that users cannot access records or functions outside their assigned permissions.  Threat DetailsARTEX is an agentic penetration testing framework originally released on GitHub by the developer "Autumn-27". It orchestrates multiple LLM backends to autonomously perform reconnaissance, vulnerability identification, and exploitation, significantly lowering the technical barrier for conducting complex intrusion campaigns.The threat actor configured ARTEX to use the following AI backends:BackendRoleDeepSeek v4.1-flashPrimary LLM BackendZhipu AI GLM-5.3Supplementary ReasoningSpaceXAI Grok 4.6Supplementary ReasoningTable 1: AI backends configured in ARTEX and their roles in the campaign. Following public disclosure of the abuse, the ARTEX developer made the project closed source. However, previously downloaded copies and forks may remain available. How it WorksThe campaign unfolds in four phases from ARTEX-assisted reconnaissance and exploitation to data theft and monetization planning.Reconnaissance: ARTEX agents autonomously identified and probed peripheral internet-facing web applications outside the institutions’ core banking infrastructure, including customer-facing inquiry portals and employee-facing mobile application backends.Exploitation: LLM-driven agents identified and exploited vulnerabilities including SQL injection and authentication bypass in the peripheral web applications to gain unauthorized access.Data exfiltration: Stolen records included full names, phone numbers, annual income figures, and loan limits. This information could support subsequent financial fraud and social engineering.Monetization planning: The threat actor used Claude Code sessions to seek advice on selling stolen South Korean financial PII and to locate Korean-language Telegram channels used to sell stolen data.Attack chainThe attack chain below illustrates the four phases of the campaign.Figure 1: ARTEX attack chain, from reconnaissance and exploitation to data exfiltration and monetization planning. ARTEX architecture and agent workflowARTEX uses an orchestration layer, known as a harness, to coordinate its models and agents. The harness provides the model with the current task state and previous results. The model selects the next action, a worker executes the selected tool against the target, and the results are returned to the model to inform subsequent actions.The planner divides the engagement into tasks, while worker agents execute tools and store findings, and the reporting component generates a report containing validated findings.The harness supported multiple LLM backends. In this campaign, the threat actor configured ARTEX to use the services listed in Table 1.ARTEX guardrails and scope controlsARTEX included guardrails intended to restrict targeting of government entities and universities through a default blocklist. However, these restrictions did not extend to financial institutions, as shown in ARTEX’s source code below.Figure 2: ARTEX source code defining default government and education domain filters.  Behavioral IndicatorsThe following table outlines potential indicators defenders can investigate alongside other evidence of suspicious activity. IndicatorDescriptionOutbound API calls to api.anthropic.com, api.deepseek.com, open.bigmodel.cn, or api.x.aiPotential use of LLM services; investigate unexpected calls in conjunction with other suspicious activityHigh-frequency automated HTTP requests with sequential enumeration patterns against login and search endpointsPotential automated reconnaissance or enumerationOutbound transfers of structured data including names, phone numbers, and financial information over HTTPS to unauthorized external destinationsPotential exfiltration of financial PIIPresence of *.aspx or *.jsp files in unexpected web application pathsPotential web shell activityTable 2: Potential behavioral and file-based indicators associated with the techniques described in this campaign.  ConclusionThe threat actor used ARTEX to support reconnaissance and exploitation in targeting South Korean financial institutions. The ARTEX agents identified and probed peripheral, internet-facing web applications, then exploited vulnerabilities in those applications to gain unauthorized access. ThreatLabz encourages organizations to follow the recommendations in this blog, such as reducing application exposure and deploying deception controls, to strengthen defenses against AI-assisted attacks. How Zscaler Can HelpStageRecommended MitigationMinimize the external attack surfaceEliminate externally exposed assets like enterprise applications which are often subject to these zero-day exploitation attempts by leveraging a Zero Trust architecture.Perform red teaming on all external assets. Zscaler’s AI red teaming uses an agentic workflow with controls designed to support authorized security testing:Start with the application’s source code to map the agent’s tools, permissions, inputs, and access checks. Our agents then test specific security hypotheses.Update the testing plan after each finding. Each agent has a defined role and access only to that role’s tools. Shared memory tracks roles, trust boundaries, and data flows. This supports testing whether a user, such as a broker, can access another broker’s client files.Enforce rules of engagement in the harness rather than relying on model instructions alone.Prevent compromiseDetonate unknown second-stage payloads with Advanced Cloud Sandbox.Route server egress through ZIA to detect/block post-compromise activity.Enable SSL/TLS inspection for all traffic, including trusted sources.Enable Advanced Threat Protection to block known C2 domains.Use Advanced Cloud Firewall to extend C2 controls across all ports/protocols, including emerging C2.Prevent lateral threat movementUse ZPA to enforce least-privilege user-to-app segmentation for crown-jewel apps (employees and third parties).Use ZPA inline inspection to block exploitation attempts against private apps from compromised users.Use Zscaler Deception to detect and contain lateral movement or privilege escalation with decoy assets and accounts.Prevent data lossInspect outbound traffic across channels with Zscaler DLP. items.title: Suspected TraderTraitor Group Uses Trojanized Terraform Provider to Deliver Cross-Platform Malware
items.summary:
IntroductionIn July 2026, Zscaler ThreatLabz uncovered a campaign linked to TraderTraitor (also tracked as Jade Sleet, UNC4899, Pressure Chollima, and Slow Pisces), an advanced persistent threat actor backed by the North Korean government that has targeted the cryptocurrency industry for years. This campaign also significantly overlaps with the previously reported KelpDAO incident, the analysis of which discussed both FLATROOF and ROOFDECK, two malware families also observed in this campaign. The attackers utilized a trojanized Terraform provider to deliver a Bash loader that selects and downloads malware tailored to the victim's operating system. The FLATROOF malware deployed Python scripts to steal sensitive data from the victim before ultimately dropping the ROOFDECK backdoor to gain full remote control.In this blog, ThreatLabz examines the inner workings of these tools and analyzes the multi-stage infection chain. We also explore how this sophisticated malware conceals and retrieves its final command-and-control (C2) address to evade detection. Key TakeawaysIn July 2026, ThreatLabz discovered a trojanized Terraform provider that executes malicious code as soon as Terraform loads the provider.The trojanized Terraform provider downloads a cross-platform Bash loader from a HashiCorp-themed lookalike domain while preserving normal Terraform behavior.The loader selects payloads for macOS, Linux, and Windows according to the operating system and CPU architecture.Encrypted executables are appended to decoy .woff files and recovered using marker-based extraction and AES-256-CBC decryption.The delivered FLATROOF variant is a Rust-based cross-platform backdoor with platform-specific persistence and redundant C2 channels.The FLATROOF Python stealers target browser credentials, cookies, terminal history, system information, and cryptocurrency wallet extensions.The subsequent backdoor named ROOFDECK uses layered C2 discovery through local configuration, a cryptographically signed Pastebin dead drop, and Nostr profile metadata. Attack ChainThe figure below illustrates the attack chain, from the execution of the trojanized Terraform provider through FLATROOF deployment, data theft, and installation of the ROOFDECK backdoors. Figure 1: Infection chain delivering FLATROOF and ROOFDECK through a trojanized Terraform provider. Technical AnalysisWhile this analysis was being prepared for publication, SentinelLabs independently reported related TraderTraitor activity involving weaponized Terraform projects, FLATROOF, and ROOFDECK malware. Their research provides detailed insight into the social engineering and initial intrusion aspects of the campaign. Our analysis focuses on the internal implementation of the malicious Terraform provider and its cross-platform payload delivery mechanism.Trojanized Terraform providerThe initial payload identified by ThreatLabz is written in Go and named terraform-provider-awsbeta_v1.0.0. It masquerades as an Amazon Web Services (AWS) provider for HashiCorp Terraform. Terraform providers are executable plugins loaded by Terraform to communicate with infrastructure platforms and services. Although it remains unclear how the trojanized Terraform provider was delivered to the victim, Terraform provider binaries execute on developer workstations and CI/CD systems. This suggests that the campaign may target cloud engineers or developers who use Terraform.The binary’s Go symbols reveal a functional provider scaffold under terraform-provider-awsbeta/internal/provider, including example resource and data source implementations. The threat actor added a malicious sibling package named awsbeta and called its exported routine directly from main. As a result, the malicious code executes when Terraform starts the provider.The provider uses a file named session.lock in the system temporary directory as a run-once marker. If the marker is absent, the provider:Determines the temporary directory using TMPDIR, falling back to /tmp.Downloads a second-stage payload over HTTPS.Writes a Bash payload to a file named safari_updater in the temporary directory.Adds executable permissions to the file.Launches it through sh -c as a detached child process.Creates the lock file to prevent repeated execution.The download URL uses the lookalike domain hashicorp-terraform[.]io and a path resembling a legitimate Terraform plugin metrics endpoint. Meanwhile, the provider continues to respond as expected, which may make the compromise less noticeable to the victim.Cross-platform Bash loaderThe downloaded safari_updater file is a Bash script that supports macOS, Linux, and Windows systems running a compatible Unix-like shell environment such as Cygwin, MinGW, or MSYS.The script maps each operating system to a font family and each architecture to a font style to construct the filename for the next-stage payload. Linux uses NotoSansCJK, macOS uses HiraginoSans, and Windows uses the MalgunGothic font name for the next-stage payload. Architectures are represented by style names such as Bold (x86_64, amd64), Regular (aarch64, arm64), ExtraBold (ARMv7, ARMv6), or Italic (32-bit x86). The resulting filename resembles a normal web font file, such as HiraginoSans-Regular.woff on a macOS system with an ARM64 processor. The encrypted payloads are disguised as font files and are downloaded from a public source. For example, a GitHub repository hosting the next-stage payloads is shown in the figure below.Figure 2: Attacker-controlled GitHub repository hosting encrypted payloads disguised as font files.Payloads are written to paths that resemble those of legitimate application components, as listed in the table below. Note that the directories are created if they do not already exist.PlatformPayload PathLinux$HOME/.config/git/updatemacOS$HOME/Library/com.apple.iTunesCloud/SystemUpdateWindows$HOME/AppData/Local/Microsoft/Edge/service.exeTable 1: Operating system-specific payload storage locations for FLATROOF.The loader attempts to download the payload from three sources in sequence: a dynamic DNS host, a GitHub repository, and a Vercel-hosted site. The use of public hosting and URL paths that resemble font caches may help malicious traffic blend with ordinary developer and web activity.Each downloaded .woff file contains decoy font data followed by the marker @@ENDFONT@@ and an encrypted executable. The loader extracts the data after the marker, Base64 decodes it, and decrypts it with AES-256-CBC using the key PTa3WZPQZAjj55t@. To maximize compatibility, the loader can decrypt the payload via Python, Node.js, Perl, or OpenSSL depending on the software that is installed on the infected system. On macOS, the script removes the quarantine attribute using the xattr -d com.apple.quarantine command and applies an ad hoc code signature before execution.FLATROOF cross-platform backdoorThe decrypted payloads for macOS, Linux, and Windows share the same Rust source module layout and core functionality. ThreatLabz assesses that the malware is consistent with the FLATROOF family described in the KelpDAO incident.FLATROOF decrypts its embedded configuration using the key u73adF39ZT with PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256, followed by AES-256-GCM decryption. The JSON configuration defines platform-specific installation paths, persistence mechanisms, polling intervals, and C2 communication channels, as shown in the example below.{
 "aes_key": "a9d932dcfa3289a6",
 "github_polling_interval": 60,
 "github_repo": "xxx",
 "github_token": "ghp_xxx",
 "init_python_enable": false,
 "main_base_url": "hxxps://arusupport-region1-webhook[.]online/statics/cache/v11/abicfjej",
 "main_upload_url": "https://www.example.com",
 "payload_path_linux": ".config/snap/imagent",
 "payload_path_macos": "Library/Services/imagent",
 "payload_path_win": "AppData/Local/Microsoft/Windows/PowerShell/config.exe",
 "persist_enable": true,
 "persist_name_linux": "snap-imagent",
 "persist_name_macos": "imagent",
 "persist_name_win": "powershell-config-service",
 "persist_type_linux": "service",
 "persist_type_macos": "zlogout",
 "persist_type_win": "reg",
 "tg_room_id": -1003[redacted]807,
 "tg_token": "8757853278:[redacted]dKI91AvprMdUkqOLAq37AOKg"
}The analyzed variants support three C2 mechanisms:Telegram Bot API for command retrieval and exfiltration of command results or files.GitHub API polling using a configured repository and token (not configured in the variant shown above).An attacker-controlled HTTP webhook for registration and tasking.Not every channel was configured in every sample, but the shared code supports multiple communication channels, providing redundancy and potentially allowing malicious traffic to blend in with traffic to widely used services.FLATROOF also implements platform-specific persistence mechanisms. The configuration references a service on Linux, a shell logout mechanism on macOS, and a registry Run value on Windows. Its command set supports system discovery, process and file management, command execution, payload download, data upload, persistence management, configuration changes, and self-removal.Embedded Python information stealersFLATROOF uses operating system-specific Python scripts to collect and package host and browser artifacts into a compressed archive for exfiltration. The Linux and macOS scripts stage data in temp/collected_data before creating temp/collected_data.zip, while the Windows script archives files from a directory named data into collected_data.zip and removes local staging files afterward.All three scripts target browser profile artifacts that can contain saved credentials, cookies, browsing history, and autofill data:Chromium-based browser databases: History, Cookies, Login Data, and Web DataFirefox browser databases: places.sqlite, cookies.sqlite, logins.json, key4.db, formhistory.sqlite, and addons.jsonCommand and shell historyList of installed applications and running processes, system information, and the current usernameThe scripts also include platform-specific capabilities for stealing sensitive data from each targeted operating system, as shown in the table below.PlatformAdditional CapabilitiesLinuxRetrieves the Chrome Safe Storage secret through the Linux Secret Service, copies local keyring files, and gathers OS and CPU information. macOSCollects Safari history, bookmarks, cookies, and extension names, as well as the user’s login.keychain-db file.WindowsCollects Chrome, Edge, and Brave browser data, Windows Credential Manager entries, PowerShell and Command Prompt history, and locally stored browser extension data for the cryptocurrency wallets MetaMask, Phantom, Trust Wallet, and Rabby. Table 2: Operating system-specific capabilities across Python scripts.Additionally, the Windows script contains two embedded native payloads. The first is a 64-bit Windows executable that is decoded using the XOR key 0x37 and injected into a suspended Chromium process to recover master encryption keys. The recovered keys are saved to [browser name]_aes.txt for staging. The second component, dropped as cookie_copy_tool.exe, copies cookie data when standard database copy operations fail.The Python script’s verbose comments, use of emojis, repetitive exception handling, and inconsistent naming conventions suggest that portions of the code may have been generated or modified with the assistance of a large language model (LLM), as shown in the figure below.Figure 3: Python script showing indications of code generated using AI.ROOFDECK backdoorThreatLabz also identified Windows and macOS variants of ROOFDECK that are likely related to this campaign. ROOFDECK's most distinctive feature is its resilient C2 discovery process. The malware first reads a local configuration file disguised as a legitimate application file. It can then retrieve a Pastebin file containing an encrypted server address and an RSA signature separated by ||.ROOFDECK verifies the signature before decrypting and accepting the server address. This prevents a third party from modifying the Pastebin file to redirect infected systems without the operator’s signing key. If the Pastebin lookup fails, ROOFDECK can query Nostr profile metadata. The malware contains a set of attacker-controlled public identities and relay servers, expands the relay list through a public directory, and reads the website field from profile events. At the time of analysis, an active profile named tulip pointed to the same Pastebin URL embedded in the Windows variant, as shown in the figure below.Figure 4: Attacker-controlled Nostr profile and metadata used to locate the current Pastebin URL for C2 discovery.This layered design provides several ways to obtain the C2 server address:Use the locally stored address.Retrieve a signed and encrypted address from Pastebin.Use Nostr metadata to locate the current dead-drop Pastebin URL.Once the server address is resolved, ROOFDECK communicates with the server over HTTP and WebSocket endpoints.The Windows and macOS variants implement nearly identical functionality, including:Host, process, disk, and filesystem discoveryExecution of individual shell commands and access to an interactive reverse shellFile creation, deletion, movement, compression, download, and uploadClipboard read and write operationsBackground task managementPersistence installation, removal, and status checksChanges to C2 and polling settingsAgent updates, version checks, and destruction Threat AttributionPublic reporting indicates that this campaign targets cryptocurrency and Web3 developers through trojanized developer tools that deliver cross-platform malware—tactics consistent with activity previously attributed to TraderTraitor.Similar campaigns have leveraged trojanized applications, Python packages, and social engineering via fraudulent job offers. The use of FLATROOF and ROOFDECK malware also overlaps with findings reported in the KelpDAO incident.ThreatLabz identified substantial overlap in tactics and targeting with TraderTraitor. However, ThreatLabz has not identified unique code similarities, shared infrastructure, or cryptographic links sufficient to independently attribute this campaign to TraderTraitor with high confidence. ConclusionThis campaign highlights how threat actors abuse trusted developer workflows through trojanized Terraform providers to deliver cross-platform malware across macOS, Linux, and Windows systems. FLATROOF and ROOFDECK provide extensive capabilities for credential theft and persistent access. ROOFDECK also supports resilient C2 discovery through signed Pastebin files and Nostr metadata. Organizations should restrict the use of untrusted Terraform providers, verify provider checksums, and monitor for unexpected process activity to reduce the risk of developer workstation compromise.
